parts.passage:
You will hear a woman asking a sales assistant about insurance policies.

Assistant: Good morning, take a seat. I see you’ve picked up some of our brochures.

Customer: Yes, I’ve been reading the one on travel.

Assistant: Would the travel insurance be for you or for your family as well?

Customer: Just for me.

Assistant: So, individual1?

Customer: That’s right.

Assistant: Are you looking for a basic or a comprehensive policy?

Customer: To be honest, I’ve had basic in the past, but it didn’t pay out very much.

Assistant: That’s often true. With our company, you can be insured for different amounts. For instance, in Section 1, baggage and personal effects, you can be insured for all five subsections or for as few as two.

Customer: I think I’d like insurance for all five since I’m going to some unsafe places.

Assistant: Wise decision. By the way – can a camera be counted as a single item2, or must it be included in cameras and portable electronic equipment3?

Assistant: If you have an expensive camera, you can nominate it as a single item; our maximum payout is $1,500. Occasionally, people have their camera and computer stolen together. If insurance is only taken out on subsection two, this may not cover the replacement of both things. That’s what

Customer: happened with my previous policy. However, in that one, there was a higher limit for lost or stolen money. Yours is only $7004.

Assistant: These days, with credit cards, people don’t carry much cash, so we’ve set the limit accordingly. Still, we pay out well for documents.

Customer: Indeed – in the disrupted travel section, rational costs5 is written for a missed connection or an early return instead of an amount of money. What exactly are rational costs?

Assistant: Put it this way: if you miss your flight due to poor weather that is verifiable, we pay $300 per day of lost time. If you arrive at check-in as the aircraft is leaving because you overslept, we still pay out, but only $100 a day. We rely on information from the airline6 to determine this.

Assistant: Are you also interested in vehicle insurance?

Customer: Yes, I am. I’m about to buy a nice old car – a vintage Jaguar XJ6.

Assistant: Hey, I used to have one of those, although nowadays I prefer old motorbikes. Did you know you can insure a vehicle on its own, or you can include it in our Multi-saver policy along with your house and contents?

Customer: Yes, I saw that. It’s true, I’m buying an expensive car, but I rent my house, so I’m not ready for a Multi-saver – that benefits homeowners.

Assistant: I understand. Have you decided which level of cover you’d like for your car? Top Cover?

Customer: Top Cover.

Assistant: Are you sure? It is pricey.

Customer: I know, but last time I had insurance, I wasn’t covered for storm damage.

Assistant: Don’t tell me that was just before the November hailstorm.

Customer: Aha – so I need storm damage insurance. Also, I’d like my policy to start as soon as I’ve paid for it. With my old one, there was a stand-down period of two weeks – could you believe I backed into a wall just three days after I’d taken out the policy? Oh dear. Then I spent months fighting with the insurance company over the value of my car. I know it wasn’t worth much, but it was relatively new.

Assistant: If you choose Top Cover, we agree on a value for your car and renegotiate each year to avoid disputes. Again, it’s not as cheap as some, but the policy works out better in the long run.

parts.passage:
You will hear a man introducing a charity, Eyesaver, to a group of listeners.

Hello, everyone. Thanks for attending tonight’s event. Let me start with the early history of our charity. Eyesaver was founded by a retired optometrist, Timothy Gaines, 30 years ago. I have spent much of my working life at Eyesaver – I am 60 years old now, and I started working for this organisation 15 years ago, when I left a corporate position to help people with eye problems.

Now our charity has been doing various other things to help people with eye problems – that includes medication for children with eye diseases, and operational help to members of the public who have eye problems. But when Mr Gaines first founded Eyesaver, he simply wanted the program to be able to offer common eye equipment, such as glasses, to those who needed it.

We receive occasional donations from corporations and charity groups, but we have over 1,500 volunteers who collect money on the street with the little red donation boxes many of you are familiar with, and this remains the main source of our funding. Besides that, we are planning to work to secure donations from wealthy benefactors.

Many people are passionate about our cause and have been asking how to donate money to us – I really appreciate that, but our main need right now is to collect glasses for our patients. Many of you have multiple pairs of old glasses in your possession, and we encourage you to gather the pairs you no longer need and donate them to our cause. In doing this, you’ll be helping to make sure that someone else can see better.

Most of us cannot imagine a life in which we are unable to see well – this is why your glasses donations are so critical to our mission, and this is really the main purpose of our program: to show people that their donation can make a difference. As a side note, we also offer full-time positions, so let me know if you are interested.

Our goal is to make people aware that even the smallest donation can be a turning point for someone. I’m proud to say that our next program will aim at educating people about common eye diseases, so that we can help prevent many avoidable eye problems.

In order to publicise our charity, we need to do some advertising. When we first started the program, we used computers to create awareness for our cause – for instance, promoting seminars where we explained how people could help us. But in recent years, the main means of advertising our program has been through audio recordings; we’ve found this cost-efficient and effective. It’s good to know that many of our staff recommend our program to their friends and colleagues, but I’m afraid our recordings can’t show people the whole picture of our program.

Finally, I’d like to tell you about some organisations that have played important roles in the development and success of Eyesaver. Our affiliation with the National Vision Funding Group has allowed us to take our reputation to a higher level, so many more people around the country now come to us for our services.

Our association with the Eye for the Future organisation has allowed us to run cooperative advertisements through which we seek equipment manufacturers to work with us; meanwhile, some of our staff have been sent to that organisation for special training, so their skills should improve very soon.

We’ve also had a longstanding cooperation with Sam’s Eyecare Institution; our relationship with them has helped us earn support from colleges, giving us the chance to link with many different academic institutions, including colleges and universities with a good reputation.

And we have a similar friendship with a group called Youth Health, whose role has been to help us recruit and support staff. We plan to contact some colleges too, and hope that with their help more college students will get to know our program.

So, as you can see, we have all bases covered in linking with students. Thank you so much for your attention today – we will appreciate your donations, no matter how large or small.

You will hear a professor talking to her student, Rangi, about his study options.

Professor Anderson: Come in, Rangi.

Rangi: Thank you, Professor Anderson. I’ve been meaning to contact you, but I just got back last night.

Professor Anderson: Where have you been?

Rangi: Conferences in Massachusetts and New York.

Professor Anderson: Physics conferences? Great – I’m looking forward to attending conferences like that one day myself. I imagine that won’t be so far away for you – I was extremely impressed with your Classical Mechanics exam. In fact, you were one of only two students out of 180 to get an A plus.

Rangi: Wow, I really did enjoy that course.

Professor Anderson: So, how can I help you?

Rangi: I’m sorry to say it’s a bit of a long story. You see, I’ve had to rethink my studies completely, and I wonder if I’m making the right decision.

Professor Anderson: You’re doing two degrees – science and arts.

Rangi: I was doing two, but I’ve decided to focus on science. It all came about because I wanted to study abroad for a year – I was thinking about Edinburgh. Firstly, I sought approval from the maths and physics departments; I wanted to take quantum mechanics and computer simulations at Edinburgh.

Professor Anderson: Those are third-year courses, right?

Rangi: Yeah, so I received approval from maths and physics, but the stumbling block was the higher authority – the science faculty. When I submitted my application, it was rejected. It turns out that students who study abroad for a year can only take first- or second-year courses, or third-year courses in a subject that isn’t their major. I’d never heard that before, and needless to say, neither had the lecturers who approved my transfer, nor does the regulation appear anywhere on the science faculty’s website.

Professor Anderson: That’d be right – that faculty has an unclear timetable for students.

Rangi: So then I thought I’d take arts courses at Edinburgh instead, and leave the third-year maths until I came back. I quickly got approval for second-year history and philosophy from the arts faculty.

Professor Anderson: When are you heading off?

Rangi: That’s just it – during this process, I began to think carefully about my studies. To be honest, the arts courses I’d done were less challenging than the science ones, so I’ve decided to drop arts. Doing that means I’ll finish my science degree earlier.

Professor Anderson: Where do I figure in all this?

Rangi: The first week after I made my decision, I felt fine without the arts courses, but this week I’ve had some doubts. When I started the two degrees, lecturers in the science faculty assured me that scientists these days need a rounded education, which they get if they take some arts courses. I was even told I’d learn to write and think better if I did philosophy.

Professor Anderson: I do think the claims made by some lecturers are doubtful.

Rangi: Then there’s the fact that now I’m going to be stuck here next year – I was so excited about going to Europe, and it’s disappointing to give that up.

Professor Anderson: It is disappointing to give that up. Still, the reason I wanted to contact you, Rangi, is that I’m looking for students to work six hours a week in my lab. It’s paid work – not highly paid, but probably better than working in a bar – and we’ve just bought a new laser, which you’d learn to use.

Rangi: That sounds excellent. As to going abroad…

Professor Anderson: Why not do your postgraduate studies in the US instead? There’s some amazing physics being done in Massachusetts – if you like, I can send you the papers from the conference. Of course, I’d be sad to lose you if you did go abroad, but an A-plus student like you has a very good chance of winning a major scholarship.

Rangi: Goodness, I’ve never even considered that.

Professor Anderson: Personally, I think committing yourself to science is the way to go.

Rangi: Thanks, Professor Anderson – you’ve taken a load off my mind. Now I don’t have to deal with Hegel any more; I have plenty of time to read those conference papers instead.

parts.passage:
You will hear part of a lecture about leatherback turtles.

Today I’m going to talk about the leatherback turtle. Dr Jeanette Wyneken of Florida Atlantic University has shown that the advantageous streamlined shape31 of leatherback turtles allows them to swim more efficiently than other species, using less force to travel the same distance as other sea turtles of comparable size and weight. In fact, leatherback turtles spend on average 20% less energy40 than other deep-diving animals.

The champions of deep diving have always been assumed to be marine mammals – the great whales and seals – but recent research suggests that leatherback sea turtles may also rank among the ocean’s greatest air-breathing divers, and are in fact one of the deepest-diving reptiles. In one remarkable dive recorded near St Croix in the US Virgin Islands, scientists tracked a 650-pound female that sank to more than 3,930 feet and remained there for 37 minutes.

High pressure poses a real challenge for deep divers – the strong forces involved could compress the chest, causing broken bones or tissue damage. Unlike its hard-shelled relatives, the leatherback has a shell that is soft33 rather than bony, made up of widely separated ribs buried in thick tissue, with the whole structure overlaid with a leathery skin.

How do deep-diving animals such as whales, seals, penguins and leatherback turtles avoid decompression sickness and other hazards while diving to great depth39s, and even while sleep34ing for long periods of time? Thanks to the sheer size of their lungs, leatherbacks can sleep in the water for several hours at a stretch. Many of the deepest-diving marine mammals also take a small breath and forcefully exhale before diving, in addition to reducing their buoyancy so that they can dive more easily; this severely limits the amount of nitrogen in their bloodstream.

One reason the leatherback ranges so far may be its specialised diet: this giant of the sea feeds mainly on jellyfish, which are full of a high proportion of protein35 and other useful minerals it requires. Jellyfish and related prey are largely ignored and eaten by few other animals, which, as one might suspect, means a lifetime of eating mostly jellyfish requires some special adaptations to make the job easier.

During the 1994 and 1995 nesting seasons, with the help of scientists, recorders were attached to ten female leatherbacks that had just laid eggs. As a result, researchers were able to monitor their migration36 pattern in the Atlantic Ocean when they returned to the sea. Some of the longest journeys recorded for any animal have been made by this marine turtle: in 1990, a female leatherback was tagged when she nested in Suriname, on the north-east coast of South America, and less than one year later she was captured off the coast of Ghana, in West Africa, having travelled 3,700 miles across the Atlantic Ocean.

Upon returning to the surface37, the turtles take a quick breath and immediately head straight back down again – no time is given to sleep or rest. Scientists can only start tracking a turtle once it reaches the surface, and on closer examination they noticed a difference in dives32 depending on the time of day: night dives are shallower, with less depth, than day dives.

Leatherbacks are such strong swimmers that they rarely stop moving, a behaviour that has made it impossible to keep them in captivity. Their front flippers are more than half the length of their body, and generate power38 from huge muscles which can account for 30% of the animal’s total body weight.

Since leatherbacks cannot easily be studied in captivity, researchers have developed new methods for studying them at sea: an instrument capable of recording both location and depth, developed at a physiological research laboratory, has been used to study these diving marine animals. Scientists soon realised the turtles were probably diving so much in order to follow their food source.

In tropical waters, jellyfish are most common at a biological zone known as the deep scattering layer; this consists of a layer of zooplankton that hovers below 1,800 feet during the day and migrates to the surface at night.
